claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films or nanoribbons possess inherent nanoscale residual strain.
Defects in the as-deposited material produce magnetic pinning.
Controlled post-deposition annealing will relieve localized nanoscale strain.
A moderate-temperature anneal can relieve strain without significant grain growth or phase transformation.
Residual strain acts as a magnetic pinning site at grain boundaries and interfaces.
Defect-induced grain-boundary and interfacial roughness acts as a magnetic pinning site.
Residual strain and interfacial defects mediate magnetoelastic coupling in this alloy system.
Annealing relaxes disordered regions in the films or nanoribbons.
Reducing local strain diminishes magnetoelastic domain-wall pinning.
Reduced domain-wall pinning permits more reversible magnetic-domain reorientation under low applied fields.
Annealed samples will have narrower magnetization loops and lower magnetic hysteresis than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will shift the magnetocaloric temperature change relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The shifted magnetocaloric temperature change will reflect a more efficient and reversible magnetization process.
Heat-transfer limitations materially affect the measured magnetocaloric response during nanoscale cycling.
Strain-associated magnetic pinning causes pronounced hysteresis in the as-deposited baseline.
The as-deposited baseline can exhibit a bulk-like magnetocaloric response.
A bulk-like magnetocaloric response may weaken in low-dimensional thin films or nanoribbons.
The proposed effects apply in low-field, nanoscale operating regimes where heat-transfer-rate limits are significant.
Confinement and interfacial phenomena may influence hysteresis and the magnetocaloric response independently of strain relaxation.
